article_title: VS Code 1.148 Tests a Rust-Based WebAssembly Diff Algorithm, Citing a 2x Median Speedup, and Shrinks Its CLI by 40%

content_preview.title: VS Code 1.148 Tests a Rust-Based WebAssembly Diff Algorithm, Citing a 2x Median Speedup, and Shrinks Its CLI by 40%
content_preview.summary: VS Code 1.148 adds an opt-in Rust/WebAssembly diff algorithm Microsoft says is twice as fast at the median, and ships a CLI about 40% smaller.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

Visual Studio Code 1.148, released November 25, 2026, adds an experimental diff algorithm written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly, which [Microsoft's release notes](https://code.visualstudio.com/updates/v1_148) say computes diffs "more than 2× faster at the median across all diffs, with noticeably fewer slow-tail timeouts" in early rollout measurements. editor_notes.content_quality: Clean, well-organized News piece (761 words, within the 400-1200 range). Overview/What We Know/What We Don't Know structure is used correctly: the lead states the two headline figures (2x median speedup, 40% CLI size reduction) with explicit attribution to Microsoft's own release notes, and the closing section explicitly flags that both figures are vendor-reported ('early rollout measurements') with no independent benchmark yet. No sensationalism, no AI self-reference.
editor_notes.source_verification: All 4 sources fetched successfully (status 200, no suspicious_patterns) and verified by decompressing each sha256-matched snapshot in sources/2026-11/vs-code-1148-tests-a-rust-based-webassembly-diff-algorithm-citing-a-2x-median-speedup-and-shrinks-its-cli-by-40/ (source-0.html.gz through source-3.html.gz; all four recomputed sha256 hashes matched the manifest exactly). Source-0 (code.visualstudio.com/updates/v1_148, live release-notes page) and source-1 (raw.githubusercontent.com vscode-docs v1_148.md, canonical markdown) both confirm verbatim: 'more than 2x faster at the median across all diffs, with noticeably fewer slow-tail timeouts'; 'about 40% smaller, with slight variations per platform'; 'shows when reviewing multiple heavily modified files at once in the multi-file diff editor'; 'faster connections and lower resource usage'; the @vscode/diff package name and advanced-wasm setting name. Source-2 (github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/348904, opened by hediet on Nov 17 2026) confirms verbatim every quoted criterion attributed to it: 'Correct by construction' / 'Every diff satisfies edits.apply(original) === modified, including for Unicode text' / 'No exceptions or assertion failures, and no panics in wasm'; 'At least as good as today'; 'Faster, never blocking' / 'at least as fast as advanced at p50 and p95' / 'never stalls the editor worker'; the default-switch bar '~0 and not more frequent than for advanced' / 'at most advanced's at p50 and p95' / 'not higher'; and the Done/Next checklist confirms the Insiders A/B experiment (advanced, advanced-external, advanced-wasm) is checked off (done) while 'Confirm the experiment' and the Stable-channel experiment are both still open/unchecked -- exactly as the article describes it ('still being evaluated rather than rolled out as the default in 1.148'). The issue also explicitly describes the package as '@vscode/diff npm package (built from microsoft/vscode-packages)', supporting the article's 'built from the separate microsoft/vscode-packages repository' claim. Source-3 (github.com/microsoft/vscode/pull/346266) confirms verbatim: 'unable to show a worse diff than the built-in algorithm would, so they can be rolled out through an experiment with less risk'; the onUnexpectedError fallback-on-error description; the verifyDiffSampleRate fallback-on-invalid-diff description; 'the built-in diff is shown instead'; and that only advanced-external/advanced-wasm are affected while the default advanced path is unchanged. Did a full quote-by-quote audit of every quoted string in body_markdown (17 distinct quoted phrases) against the four raw snapshots -- all 17 are verbatim matches (the only deviations are trivial sentence-initial capitalization normalization, e.g. source 'Every diff...' vs article's mid-sentence 'every diff...', which is standard editorial practice, not a misquote). No hallucinated or paraphrased-as-verbatim quotes found. Anthropic disclosure: not required - the article is about Microsoft VS Code/Rust/WebAssembly and contains no mention of Anthropic, Claude, or Claude Code in the headline, summary, lead, or body.
editor_notes.novelty_claim_verification: Independently verified, not just taken from the writer's self-reported audit. Fetched the raw markdown of the two prior Stable releases directly (curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microsoft/vscode-docs/main/release-notes/v1_147.md and v1_146.md, 575 and 409 lines respectively) and grepped both files for 'wasm', 'webassembly', '@vscode/diff', 'rust-based', '40%', 'diffAlgorithm', and CLI-size phrasing: zero matches in either file. A broader grep for bare 'diff' and 'rust' in both files turns up only unrelated hits (a notebook-diff-editor memory-leak bug fix in 1.146, and GitHub Copilot CLI session hand-off in 1.146 -- unrelated to the VS Code CLI binary). No CLI-related content at all appears in 1.147. This confirms the article's and the writer's claim that neither the WASM diff algorithm nor the 40% CLI-size reduction appeared in the two prior releases; 1.148 is their first appearance in Stable release notes. (Note: this is about first appearance in the user-facing release notes, not first appearance of any underlying code -- the GitHub tracking issue's 'Done' checklist shows incremental engineering work, e.g. bridge/Rust fixes and telemetry, landing in recent preceding PRs; the article does not claim the underlying code is brand new, only that the feature is being introduced/tested in 1.148, which is accurate.)
editor_notes.quote_audit_result: 17 of 17 quoted phrases in body_markdown verified verbatim against the raw source snapshots (see source_verification above for the full list and sources). No fabrications, no misattributions, no quotes that are actually paraphrases dressed as direct quotes.
editor_notes.speedup_figure_verification: The '2x median speedup' figure is quoted, not computed by the writer: both source-0 and source-1 state verbatim 'the WebAssembly backend computes diffs more than 2x faster at the median across all diffs, with noticeably fewer slow-tail timeouts,' explicitly attributed to Microsoft's 'early rollout measurements.' The article correctly attributes this to Microsoft rather than presenting it as an independently verified figure, and the closing 'What We Don't Know' section explicitly notes 'no independent benchmark of either change has been published yet.' This matches editorial policy on vendor figures being labelled as the vendor's.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: No unsourced claims found in the headline, summary, or lead; every number, setting name, and quote traces to one of the four cited sources. One subordinate, non-headline claim ('The VS Code CLI itself was already written in Rust prior to this release; 1.148's change is a reduction in the size of that existing Rust binary, not a rewrite into a new language') is an inference consistent with the release notes' phrasing ('The Rust-based VS Code CLI is about 40% smaller') and with VS Code's known CLI history, but is not verbatim-sourced from the four citations. It does not contradict any source and is not in the headline/summary/lead, so it does not rise to a corrections-worthy issue.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral throughout. Qualifiers ('experimental', 'opt-in', 'in early rollout measurements', 'no independent benchmark') are preserved from the sources rather than dropped, and the piece is careful to state the new diff engine is not yet the default.
editor_notes.originality: Checked src/content/articles/2026-11/ for existing VS Code coverage; no prior article in the archive covers VS Code 1.148, the @vscode/diff WASM migration, or the CLI size reduction. Not a duplicate.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Clean News submission with a full quote-by-quote audit passing on all 17 direct quotes, an independently verified novelty claim (confirmed via direct retrieval of the raw v1.147 and v1.146 release-notes markdown, not merely the writer's self-report), and correct vendor-figure attribution for both the 2x speedup and 40% size-reduction numbers. No corrections needed. Featured candidacy: 1 - solid, accurate release coverage of a widely-used developer tool for a defined developer audience; incremental rather than industry-changing.
